rationale: Zero-shot on 11 agent-harness decision points Jev beat Laya on 9 (2,100-case suite 76.7% vs 63.1%) and screened injections well (track E AUROC .98, FNR/FPR 7.0/7.0%; payloads embedded in documents detected 90.8-93.3% vs 97.5-98.3% for the DeepSeek reference), but on pre-execution safety it passed 25.5% of harmful requests (AUROC .77; Laya 81.5%), was unusable as a PII gate (FPR 63-66% vs 12-25% for the LLM reference) and both models were at chance on routing (Sec. 5; App. C Tables 3, 5, 6).

On 4,275 Turkish typed questions in seven tracks (including prompt-injection guardrails and offensive-comment moderation, whose per-track scores are only in the board file) Jev 1.13's decision-quality axis (macro-F1) was 0.851 vs 0.855-0.901 for three hosted chat LLMs and 0.761 for DeepSeek V4 Pro, while open typed models scored 0.221-0.747 and the Laya and open-jev composites (0.075-0.298) were near or below the surface-cue baseline (0.272) (Table 3, Sec. 6).

Security fine-tuning of Kev-based typed models lifted task-macro accuracy on 21,634 held-out questions to 90.34-94.51% (from 50.94-69.82%; 4B gain 26.63 pp [18.59, 30.75]), level with answer-only generative SFT (94.48% vs 94.34% at 4B, matched precision); on new sources SecJev-4B caught only 48.67% of BIPIA injections (0% FPR; generative 5.33%) and flagged 66.40% of benign IoT-23 traffic (generative 51.40%; accuracy 65.10% vs 68.10%) (Sec. 5.2-5.4; Tables 3-5).

Without task training Jev's direct binary hate-speech macro-F1 was .826/.691/.738/.960 on Dynamic/MHS/HateXplain/HateCheck vs GPT-6 Sol .897/.682/.776/.976 (commercial LLMs significantly ahead of every decision model only on Dynamic, by 4.1-5.9 points) while open typed models ranged .220-.801; all models struggled to separate hate from offensive language (3-class: Jev .532, Laya .570, Sol .604, supervised TF-IDF .639) and Jev reached .538 on conduct type (Sec. 4.1, 4.3; Tables 4-5, 8, 10).

On AgentHarm harmfulness judgments (N=97) hosted Jev reached 84.54% accuracy with ECE 0.068, against 61.86-85.57% accuracy and ECE 0.089-0.349 for the nine generative configurations: level with thinking Qwen3.8-27B (84.54%) and one point below thinking GLM-5.3-Flash (85.57%). This is a single sub-benchmark, run once, with no intervals (App. D.6, Tables 25-27). [Adjudicated: AgentHarm 84.54% vs 61.86-85.57% generative; level with best, no added condition]

As a zero-shot Noul detector, hosted Jev reached ROC-AUC 0.95-1.0 on all eight benchmarks (prompt injection, jailbreak input, harmful content, AI-generated text), with 87-99% accuracy on the six security benchmarks at a threshold fitted on 20-100 held-out calibration examples. On AI-text detection the default 0.5 threshold gave 78% mean accuracy, which rose to 89% only with the fitted threshold. Open NanoJev was near or below ROC-AUC 0.5 on three of the four tasks (Sec. V-B, Table VI, Fig. 8).

On HakemBench's Turkish guardrail track the released model caught 194/217 prompt-injection attacks but passed only 128/201 harmless look-alikes; on moderation it caught 150/157 offensive and passed 186/196 clean messages. The author flags these numbers as shaped by reading earlier test results and possibly inflated by style likeness. Its overall decision quality (macro F1 0.705) is below Jev 1.13 (0.851) and below every generative model on the board (0.741-0.901) (Secs. 4 and 6, Table 2). [Adjudicated: Macro F1 0.705 below all generative (0.741-0.901); passes 128/201 harmless look-alikes]

Zero-shot CLM-v0.1-8B scored 0.549/0.351/0.593/0.508/0.475 on RewardBench/RewardBench 2 best-of-four/RB2 pairs/RM-Bench/JudgeBench (RM-Bench and JudgeBench intervals contain chance) and gave every HaluEval item the same label (0.581, identical to always-first), while the same-size generative judge Qwen3-8B scored 0.611-0.778 with every gap significant after Benjamini-Hochberg correction; the open laya baseline sat at or near chance (0.280-0.544) (Sec. 4, Table 2).

Jev's Choice F1 was 66.1 on OLID (best Detoxify 65.7, but accuracy 74.4 vs 81.0) and 65.5 on HateXplain (Detoxify <= 57.0), and its AUROC on ModerationBench was 0.893-0.902 (0.936-0.940 with five retrieved precedents); on Facebook hate-speech policy selection (HateModerate) exact match was 29.4% without precedents and 51.6% with them, and on the PluRule test set Jev without precedents (48.4%) was below the always-'no rules broken' baseline (50.0) and published GPT-5.2 results (54.1-57.7), while Laya fell to 6.2% exact match at 100% violation recall (Tables 3-7).

As a source-support verifier for 192 GPT-4.1-mini financial calculation traces Jev reached AUROC 0.986 [0.964, 0.999] and Brier 0.034, but a zero-call signed-number-at-pointer rule nearly matched it (141 vs 142 joint passes at the 0.8 cutoff, the difference from one question); with numbers held fixed, 4 of 6 wrong-role citation swaps stayed above 0.8, and on 36 fresh pages Jev withheld 5/15 supported original citations and 11/19 equivalent alternatives (Sec. III-A, III-B, III-D; Table II, Figs. 1, 3).

Zero-shot Jev on the same 1,000-instance samples reached AUROC 0.846 for AI-generated-text detection on RAID (noul) and macro-F1 0.531 on ESCI relevance (choice), below the zero-shot macro-F1 of the generative models named in the text (Opus 5 0.609, GLM 5.3 0.593, GPT 5.6 Terra 0.573) and above most agent-built artifacts; no interval is reported for Jev and the RAID zero-shot comparators appear only in Fig. 2 (Sec. 1, 4.1-4.2, App. E).

Zero-shot on eight affective benchmarks Jev-Direct averaged 62.93% macro-F1, above five of ten LLM configurations but below the best (Gemini 3.8 Flash IO, 67.28%) and first on no dataset; it was close on English multi-label emotion (E-c 52.47 vs 52.61) and near the LLMs on Chinese CMMA emotion (21.06 vs 19.82-23.31) but far behind on humour (HD 61.80 vs 87.92), at 96.41% lower cost than Gemini IO and 250 ms median latency (Sec. 4.3, 4.5; Tables 2, 5).

The authors' Qwen3.5-4B Yes-probability verifier (BCE-trained on 2,477 examples) reached 95.24% balanced accuracy on 936 held-out reference-bound atomic judgments (untuned 84.14%), but its candidate rankings agreed with blinded human preferences on 63.49% of 126 pairs vs 60.32% for direct Qwen3.5-27B scoring (difference CI [-8.33, 16.67]) and did not lower severe identity risk in the top candidate (47.62% vs 45.24%) (Tables 2-3, Sec. 5.2-5.3).

With physical features Jev's yes/no fault question flagged 75-99% of fault windows but also 57-94% of fault-free ones (AUROC 0.65; condition answer 0.68), under the nine shift tests no model beat flagging every window (detection F1 0.71; Jev 0.67-0.70), and pooled diagnosis of consistency faults was 37% vs 46% for Qwen2.5 72B, which erred like Jev on detection (Table 5, Sec. 4.1-4.2, 4.4).

Human coders confirmed 96-100% of Jev flags (p>=0.5) where the coded field also recorded the factor but only 15% (13 flags) for unbelted occupants, 26% (27) for wrong-way driving, 52-57% for drugs and medical episodes and 71-90% for alcohol, fatigue, hydroplaning and phone use where it did not (Table B.2; Sec. 6); counts are small and intervals wide.

Unmodified Laya on Whisper ASR transcripts reached Macro F1 89.2% / AUROC 94.9% on 282 held-out robocalls and the author-adapted direct-audio Laya 99.6-100%, but spam labels are fully confounded with source corpus, and zero-shot transfer of the direct-audio variants to MInDS-14 intents stayed at the majority baseline (accuracy 6.2-8.5%, AUROC 49.0-50.8%) while urgent-clip detection at the default threshold was 9 of 20 (Tables 4.1-4.2, Sec. 4.1).

Jev's accuracy (SST-2 0.961, AG News 0.867) exceeded gpt-5.4-nano (0.948, 0.811), gpt-4.1-nano (0.938, 0.851) and the untrained DeBERTa -c in all 16 wording x rule cells (full-test estimate +5.72 [+4.70, +6.75]), but trailed the task-exposed DeBERTa on AG News (-2.30 [-3.33, -1.28]), and label descriptions alone moved the gap from +6.93 to +9.67 points (Tables 6-8, Sec. 4.3).

On 741 federal IT solicitations with quote-derived gold, Jev's primary-class accuracy 91.9% exceeded Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (89.6%) and Laya (78.0%), but on fulfillment mode (n=634) Jev reached 65.0% against Qwen's 71.0% (Laya 45.7%), with configured-build precision 0.254 (README Results table; report Sec. 9.1, 9.3).

Mean accuracy over five public classification benchmarks (CLINC150, MASSIVE ja-JP, tweet_eval emotion and sentiment, Civil Comments insult) was 83.6 for hosted Jev and 84.2 for the author's Reflex-1 against 85.6 / 84.8 for GPT-5.6 / Gemini 3.8, from one sequential run with no per-benchmark tables or intervals in the deposit (README Results table). [Adjudicated: Mean 83.6/84.2 vs 85.6/84.8 frontier LLMs on five benchmarks, no training]

Screening 142,504 records of 22 Cochrane reviews with one Noul question gave median AUC 0.9827 [IQR 0.9541, 0.9925] (above TITAN-SR's reported 0.9760), and the plugin's untuned 0.3 threshold gave pooled recall 0.9349 at specificity 0.8568, but recall reached 99% in only 16 of 22 reviews (as low as 0.6923 and 0.7778, with 16 and 22 missed includes) (report.md primary analysis tables). [Adjudicated: AUC 0.9827 > TITAN-SR, but untuned threshold >=99% recall in 16/22 reviews only]

On 4,940 ToxicChat examples at a threshold selected on 1,000 development labels, Jev reached 90.52% recall at 3.24% FPR (AP 0.8854, AUROC 0.9849) against 35.63-58.91% recall for three encoder conditions, the only arm to pass the absolute gate, but its FPR on the human-annotated negatives was 5.39% (128/2,376), above the 5% tolerance (Tables R1, R1a, R2).

The author's fine-tuned Laya with retrieval reached F1 0.89 on synthetic logs (rule baseline 0.66; 20 replications), detected 0.92 of an unseen attack, and transferred to CIC-IDS2017 SSH brute force without retuning (F1 0.98-0.99, CI lower bound 0.96 vs rule 0.76), but slow port scans were missed (recall 0.03-0.31 vs rule 0.43) because the synthetic threshold did not transfer, and recall fell to 0.00 without authentication events (Tables 1-2, 7; Sec. 5.6).

On 200 GPT-4o-generated states per task, a Jev-specific injection reached 100%/100%/97.2% ASR against hosted Jev and a universal suffix 100%/100%/97.0% (clean accuracy 100%); each template attack reached 88.5-100% on at least one task. Poisoning 5-10% of training data implanted backdoors in NanoJev with 76.1-100% target ASR while clean accuracy stayed at 90.4-94.0%. Conditional instructions in user input made hosted Jev reveal hidden gender, age group, heart-disease and ethnicity attributes with 100% coverage and accuracy (Tables I, II, V).

Reversing option order changed 1.8% of Jev's and 30.3% of Laya's decisions (53% for Laya with 60-77 labels; n=1,000), and rewording only the instructions moved accuracy by 5-15 pp per track for both systems, with the Jev-Laya ranking flipping sign in some runs on routing and RAG relevance (6/8 and 7/8) (Sec. 5, Fig. 3).

Order sensitivity was 0.039 [0.029, 0.050] for Jev 1.13 vs 0.366-0.590 for the Laya rows and 0.139 for Qwen3.5-4B read through option-letter probabilities; Jev's paraphrase agreement was 0.926 and its Turkish-minus-English Brier gap 0.009 [-0.031, 0.045], but its name-substitution slot signal 0.059 [0.020, 0.107] was above zero (possible contamination); hosted chat LLMs were not probed (Table 4, Sec. 6).

A random option permutation changed 10-17% of answers for cross-head typed models including fine-tuned Laya-large (S-PubMedBERT C 15.7%: 3% on seen tasks, 17% held-out, 28% on exams), while prior-fused (PFR, 0.3%) and bi-encoder heads were essentially invariant, so order robustness depends on the conversion and worsens under shift (Sec. 6.2; App. H).

In three open laya checkpoints the option label overrode the written definition: deleting every definition left laya-td accuracy unchanged (0.8559 vs 0.8487), a label contradicting its definition dropped it to 0.1357 (below the 0.5690 no-information control), and renaming options A/B raised PolicyBench-XF accuracy by +0.1511 [+0.1377, +0.1646]; von, which omits labels from the input, was exactly invariant, and Qwen2.5-7B and Mistral-7B label readouts showed the same effect (+0.1203, +0.1531) (Sec. 5.1-5.3, Tables 2-3).

Paraphrasing questions changed accuracy by 0.07-0.93 pp with 95.36-98.36% answer agreement (1,400 pairs per size) and permuting choice options changed it by -0.80 to +0.40 pp with 97.40-98.80% agreement (500 pairs), although 15-38 correct answers per size became wrong under paraphrase and 9B VeReMi agreement was 77% (Sec. 6.1, Table 6).

Supplying each dataset's own hate-speech definition changed 2.8-27.9% of decision-model predictions, with significant gains and losses equally frequent (8 each of 28 comparisons, 12 inconclusive); Jev was least sensitive (at most 0.5 points on Dynamic and HateCheck, -2.7 on MHS, +3.9 on HateXplain), and the policy-trained generative CoPE also lost agreement on three of four datasets (Sec. 4.2, Fig. 3; App. D).

In matched controls (20 test texts per task) neutral option identifiers cut Qwen2.5-7B's missing-answer detection by 20.0 (AG News) and 30.6 points (DBpedia), and task-aligned NONE wording raised Laya's detection by 25.0 points on Emotion, while Jev and Qwen showed zero change under the NONE wording (Sec. 3.4, Table 6).

Asking 27,367 Study 1 survey pairs in both orders flipped the winner in 8.8% of pairs (8.5% in Study 2), with a pull toward the second slot of -0.0358. Flips concentrated where confidence was low: 36.55% below p=.50 and 0.00% above .95. Forward and reversed scales correlated 0.982, and weak stochastic transitivity held in 98.37% of triples (App. B, Table 3). [Adjudicated: Order swap flips 8.8% of winners, bias -0.036; scale r=0.982; no comparator or criterion]

The order-invariant head makes order sensitivity 0.000 by construction (verified bit for bit by a permutation test). A sequential head trained with shuffled options changed 2.3-2.8% of answers under reordering at similar accuracy. Paraphrase agreement was 0.883 [0.833, 0.932] vs 0.926 [0.889, 0.963] for Jev 1.13, with overlapping intervals (Secs. 2 and 6, Table 4).

Under answer-order swap CLM flipped 0.0002 of decisions (3 flips, all exact score ties) against 0.2188 for the Qwen3-8B generative judge, and its length-preference shift was -0.023 against -0.217, but the open laya baseline flipped 0.4395 under the same swap (with most inputs truncated by its 512-token window), and CLM's order stability coexists with near-chance accuracy (Sec. 4 'Order and length stability', Table 1). [Adjudicated: Order-flip 0.0002 vs 0.2188 generative; length shift -0.023 vs -0.217]

Reordering candidates (published order, reverse and five fixed permutations, nothing else changed) changed the selected Acquire value in 46/120 node-local states and in all 120 global-interface states, with correct node-local decisions ranging 90-113/120 and global 14-90/120 across orders; the authors conclude likelihood-based candidate scoring remains order-sensitive (Sec. IV-B, Sec. VI).

Holding a 15-candidate menu token-for-token fixed, changing only the question wording moved Open-Jev-2B accuracy from 0.454 to 0.714 (26 points), and the comparative phrasing that cost Open-Jev-2B 9.4 points raised kev-0.8B from 0.622 to 0.698; putting the correct label first on a self-selected 15-candidate menu dropped kev-0.8B from 0.622 to 0.426, although at 150 labels the permutation flip rate was under 6% (Sec. 4.4, 5.4). [Adjudicated: Wording swings 26 pts, label-first -19.6 pts; shuffle <=0.6 pts, menu predictable]

With the same five precedents, replacing opaque policy identifiers by human-readable hate-speech policy names lowered Jev's binary accuracy by 5.06 points [-6.21, -3.91] and exact match by 1.64 points, while for Laya it raised binary accuracy by 2.5 points and lowered exact match by 2.0; full versus compact rendering of the same content also shifted Jev's PluRule test exact match (52.0% vs 48.4% without precedents) (Sec. 4.1, Table 4; App. A.2).

Repeating the cited column's header explicitly, with source content unchanged, moved all 8 wrong-role swap calls from accepted to withheld (B means 0.905-0.945 to 0.115-0.620) but also lowered support for equivalent citations, and on the fresh bank paired separation rose by one contrast (8/15 to 9/15) while withholding of supported originals rose from 5 to 6, so decisions depend on how the same evidence is rendered (Sec. III-C, III-D, Figs. 2-3).

Order consistency was higher for Jev than for Qwen3-32B (same answer in both presentation orders on 94.8% vs 90.6% of 500 TREC pairs and 86.7% vs 72.0% of 80,000 MS MARCO pairs), but Jev's Othello corner preference moved from 14.4% to 24.3% when the board was rendered as a coordinate list (App. G, K, N). [Adjudicated: Both-order agreement 94.8% vs 90.6% (TREC), 86.7% vs 72.0% (MS MARCO)]

On 600 held-out command questions, shuffling option order cut accuracy for Strands Decider 2B (0.59 to 0.38), Kev 9B (0.60 to 0.50) and Laya base (0.56 to 0.49) but not Clef-Flash 9B (0.54 to 0.54), and Kev 4B weapon accuracy fell 0.97 to 0.62; all zero-shot typed models but Kev 0.8B chose 'collect' 1.6-1.8 times chance among errors in either order, as did Qwen3.6 without reasoning (1.8) but less with reasoning (1.4) (Table 1, Sec. 5.1). [Adjudicated: Shuffle cuts accuracy for most typed models; collect bias 1.6-1.8x chance either order]

Rewording the three questions changed 3-6% of Jev's answers and irrelevant fields 2-6%, but class names without definitions changed 41% (ORNL consistency accuracy 71% to 6%), a same-content paraphrase of the definitions changed 8-9% and moved context-fault accuracy 13% to 43%, and shuffling state-field order changed 13% of RP-1312 answers and made the yes/no question flag 94% of fault-free windows (Sec. 4.1).

Under a preregistered paraphrase gate (Spearman rho >= 0.85 and mean |dp| <= 0.05 per feature, 200 rows), all 7 predictive TESS features passed (tightest rho 0.866, |dp| 0.0465) but 2 of 3 label-echo features failed, the paraphrase effect (mean |dp| 0.0250) was 4.4x the same-wording re-ask noise (0.0056), and on the separately preregistered Kepler transfer 3 of 6 predictive features failed rho (0.841, 0.828, 0.651) (RESULTS.md §6; RESULTS_KEPLER.md KG3 table).

Nine Jev variants crossing three question structures (12 presence nouls, one 12-way choice, hierarchical choices) with three input sizes all scored 0.912-0.919 primary-class accuracy (676-681 of 741 correct) with ECE 0.046-0.052 (report Sec. 8.2-8.3).

Yway (open XLM-R encoder with Laya's decision head, Burmese) transfers to unseen question wordings only where training wordings were broad (unseen-wording test: answerable 0.92, relevance 0.86, topic-is-X 0.89) but 'has a number' falls from 0.995 on training wordings to 0.579, the held-out register task stays at chance (0.51-0.53), and zero-shot Laya multilingual (mmBERT) scores 0.120 accuracy with ECE 0.808 on 569 Burmese topic texts against 0.863 after fine-tuning (Sec. 4.2, Table 2; Sec. 5.3-5.4, Fig. 7).

With no evidence, jev-1.13.0 Choice puts 0.83-0.93 on 'heads' under all six label sets, a pull carried by the option word (+0.354 [0.347, 0.361]) rather than key name (+0.027) or list position (-0.015) when options have descriptions; one 55%-reliable witness cuts it to +0.063, the Choice step survives three wordings (45%->55% jump 0.59-0.89), and Laya instead shows key (+0.28) and first-position (+0.15) bias (Sec. 4.1-4.2; Tables 1, 2, 6).

Reversing the option order changed the released Noma model's prediction on 9.7% [6.2, 14.8] of 186 sealed-set choice items and a seeded random reordering on 7.0% [4.1, 11.6], with accuracy unchanged (83.9% vs 84.9%) and changes concentrated on low-confidence items (mean 0.52 vs 0.90); at most 2 of 36 confident easy/original-tier items changed (Sec. 7.2; Table A5).

Trained on Norwegian and Austrian register texts, the open SignRule-Decide 4B model agreed with the AI-consensus reference on 99.3% of Austrian coalition questions and 94.6% of rule types (n=400), but on 300 Danish texts from a register never seen in training it reached 92.5% on coalitions and 62.4% on rule type, misreading Danish 'direktionen' as a collective body (Sec. 7; Tables 3, 5).

Pooled ECE was 0.143 (Jev) vs 0.158 (Laya) on tracks A-F, where Jev was confidently constant on routing (ECE 0.477), and 0.080 vs 0.198 on G-J; 26% of Laya's answers with confidence >=0.9 were wrong, and per-domain Platt scaling was needed to repair RAG calibration (ECE Laya 0.22 to 0.027, Jev 0.21 to 0.10) (Sec. 5 Calibration; App. Fig. 7).

Jev 1.13's calibration axis (1 - Brier/uniform Brier) was 0.706, equal to GLM 5.3, below Gemini 3.8 Flash (0.806) and GPT-5.6 Sol (0.727) and far above DeepSeek V4 Pro read from label log-probabilities (0.386), with post-hoc temperature 1.1058 (mildly overconfident); open typed models were poorly calibrated (Kev 0.478-0.503, Laya 0.005-0.113, open-jev 0.073) (Table 3).

After per-type temperature scaling fitted on a calibration split, seen-task top-label ECE was 3.6-4.4 for every training objective and 3.8-4.3 for the fine-tuned encoders vs 8.5-9.1 for zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-31B scaled the same way, but several models were poorly calibrated on held-out tasks and answerability questions on long clinical notes stayed near chance for most models (Sec. 6.3-6.4; Limitations; App. H).

Prefixing yes/no questions with 'Is it false that' left the returned probability essentially unchanged, so decisions flipped on 0.9656-0.9825 of items across laya checkpoints and 0.9711 for label-invariant von (laya-td accuracy 0.6419 to 0.3576), vs 0.7972 for a Qwen2.5-1.5B readout; an explicit instruction to attend to polarity did not help (0.3546) (Sec. 5.7, Fig. 5).

On the held-out security test raw ECE was 1.53-2.18% and temperature scaling improved NLL but worsened ECE (to 2.48-3.56%); on the general Kev suites the frozen security temperature did not fully recover the initialisation's confidence quality, so calibration held in-domain only (Sec. 6.3, Table 9; App. H). [Adjudicated: Low in-domain ECE after security fine-tuning; general-transfer ECE 21.10% vs 4.19% init (App. H)]

With an explicit NONE option on CLINC150, Jev rejected 63.7% of artificially omitted answers at 3.3% false rejection (Qwen2.5-7B 45.0%/3.7%, Laya 86.0%/27.7%) and its out-of-scope detection fell from 84.0% to 75.0% as candidates rose from 2 to 10 (Qwen 85.0% to 63.0%; Laya 83.0% to 99.0% at 48.8% false rejection); on DBpedia k=13 Jev detected 82.4% of missing references vs Qwen 25.0%, with none-score AUROC 0.987 [0.980, 0.994] (Sec. 3.2-3.3, Table 2).

On the 10,938 JEVal choice/noul questions Jev's ECE was 0.0532, lower than every generative configuration (0.0784 for thinking GLM-5.3-Flash to 0.2526; GPT-6-Luna 0.1159), at 78.38% accuracy (Table 1). But on 100-item tasks with analytically known distributions it put 89.35% of the mass on the true mode against 35.60% true (E_mode 53.75 pp prior, 28.12 pp posterior), the largest probability errors of all configurations evaluated (Table 2, Fig. 5, Sec. 5.1).

In-distribution, the authors' SearchJev cut mean ECE by 74.4% and 40.7% relative to same-size Qwen3.5 AR (JSON) models, and hosted Jev 1.13 kept the lowest mean ECE; on evidence sufficiency SearchJev-4B reached 96.0% accuracy vs 79.8% for Jev and 57.7% for Qwen3.5-4B AR (Table 3). On held-out datasets calibration did not transfer: SearchJev-4B's ECE was 26.9 on rewriting and 15.4 on verification, against 24.1 and 3.7 for Qwen3.5-4B AR and 5.6 and 3.7 for Jev, whose routing ECE was 20.0 (Table 5, Sec. 5.3).

Given a reject/escalate option, Jev requested new candidates for 45/48 contracts that had no valid candidate (generative LLMs 1-16/48). It escalated only 4/120 forwarding instances with no feasible path (DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 67, Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite 49, GLM-4.7-Flash 109, Qwen3.5-4B 2/120). It chose the correct placement action in 50/120 current-conflict and 11/120 resolved-conflict observation cases (Tables X and XI, Sec. VII-C).

Asked once per question, Jev had lower ECE than GPT-6 Luna's token probabilities on all eight human-labelled reading tasks (e.g. V-Dem 0.057 vs 0.390, difference 0.333 [0.318, 0.347]) and higher AUROC on seven of eight. But Qwen3.8-27B was better calibrated on the four pairwise tasks (survey pairs 0.049 vs 0.109, difference -0.060 [-0.091, -0.009]), and the gap to Luna disappeared when probabilities were averaged over both presentation orders (Fig. 2, Tables 9-10, App. B).

Temperature scaling lowered smooth ECE on the support development set (0.050 to 0.038) but raised it on held-out support questions (0.027 to 0.045 for Run 1, which never trained on them). The guardrail track had smooth ECE 0.158 vs 0.025-0.084 on other tracks, and the 'not sure' signal let 18 wrong answers through out of 148 guardrail answers at confidence >=0.99 (0.122 [0.078, 0.184]). The board calibration axis was 0.482, below Jev 1.13 (0.706), GLM 5.3 (0.706), GPT-5.6 Sol (0.727) and Gemini 3.8 Flash (0.806) but above DeepSeek V4 Pro (0.386) and Qwen3.5-4B (0.438) (Sec. 5, Tables 1-2). [Adjudicated: Guardrail ECE 0.158, 12.2% wrong at >=0.99; other tracks 0.025-0.084]

Raw CLM confidence was overconfident by +0.235 to +0.401 (ECE 0.235-0.402); one pooled temperature (20.1) fitted on a 30% calibration split brought ECE to 0.032-0.062 on all six benchmarks, but the repaired confidence ranked CLM's own errors above chance on only 3 of 6 benchmarks (AUROC 0.587-0.609; RM-Bench 0.487, HaluEval 0.495) (Sec. 5, Table 3).

With an explicit ABSTAIN candidate on 60 held-out cases (half with no valid candidate), the Jev-style Shared-KV readout on Qwen2.5-3B rejected 28/30 no-valid cases but chose the correct value in only 17/30 valid cases (45/60 overall) against 51/60 for autoregressive generation, and the authors conclude candidate scores cannot be treated as reliable confidence and safe rejection is unresolved (Sec. IV-F).

Across seven open typed families the first-pass probabilities were systematically too high after a menu change (predicting accuracy from them erred by 21.0 points against 1.33 for the argmax-based predictor), and averaging order-permuted passes cut ECE from 0.09 at K=1 to 0.03 at K=2 (67%) while changing accuracy by a pooled 1.2 points, so usable calibration required extra passes (Sec. 4.2, 5.1).

SanSi (the authors' looped open typed model) separated items with and without key evidence at AUROC 0.935 and gave a hard answer to 17.5% of 382 unanswerable items (Jev API, not trained for this target, 62.8%), but confidence rose on wrong as well as right answers (0.567 to 0.660), error AUROC rose only from 0.760 to 0.795, 19.7% of loop-8 errors had confidence >= 0.9, and ECE (0.093; Jev API 0.066) fell to 0.022-0.029 only with a temperature fitted on labelled development data (Sec. 5.3, 6; App. F.3-F.4, Tables 23-25).

Jev's Noul probabilities had ECE 14.9% (OLID) and 33.2% (HateXplain) without precedents and 9.7% and 20.2% with them, and on held-out PluRule its Choice confidence was overconfident by 12.2 points without precedents (ECE 12.8%) and 5.4 with them, with correctness AUC 0.612-0.728; Laya was underconfident by 7.3-20.7 points with correctness AUC down to 0.500 (App. B.1 Table 13, App. D.2 Table 16).

On 12,280 held-out chess move pairs with a non-tied Stockfish preference, Jev had the lowest ECE against Stockfish (0.081 vs DiffusionGemma 0.159, OLMo-2-32B 0.176, Qwen3-32B 0.260), although agreement was near chance for all judges (Jev 54.5%, others 52.9-54.4%) (Sec. 5.5).

Zero-shot typed models had command ECE 0.10-0.57 and confidence AUROC 0.45-0.89 (fixed order) with no link between calibration and sensitivity; typed-decisions Laya, Strands and Kev 9B were under-confident (mean top probability 0.31-0.42 at accuracy 0.59-0.60), and the most sensitive model (Laya base, AUROC 0.89 [0.85, 0.92]) was at chance within categories (0.52 [0.40, 0.63]) and fell to 0.72 with shuffled options (Table 2, Sec. 5.2).

On 43,496 Chinese-language typed questions, the authors' Chip (Kev-0.8B fine-tuned on 88,604 records) had ECE 0.0032 and hosted JEV 0.0271 vs 0.0307-0.0607 for three flagship LLMs' stated probabilities (Gemma3 0.0225 on its valid records), but Chip's calibration did not transfer to JevBench (ECE 0.1633 Original, 0.3577 Hard vs JEV 0.0947) (Tables 3-4). [Adjudicated: Chip ECE 0.0032 needs target fine-tuning; JevBench ECE 0.163/0.358]

Pooled shifted ECE was 0.27 [0.21, 0.36] for Jev vs 0.43 for Qwen2.5 72B, 0.60 for 7B and 0.36 for LightGBM, and did not drift under shift (+0.01 [-0.09, 0.09]), but windows at stated 0.94 were right 62% of the time, temperature scaling (0.28 to 0.17) overshot into underconfidence, the yes/no and condition answers contradicted each other (84% 'fault' vs 95% 'normal' on ORNL fault-free windows), and Jev gave its top answer >=0.7 on 63% of fault windows with no physical trace (Sec. 4.2, 4.4, 4.6, Fig. 4).

Jev's raw probabilities overstated the human rate so that the identity map failed the held-out unbiasedness rule for 14 of 15 factors (all but vehicle defects); Platt or isotonic maps fitted on 2,309 judgments cut held-out Brier (x1000), e.g. alcohol 4.56 to 2.71 and hit-and-run 7.44 to 5.84, and the recalibrated counts then agreed with an independent blinded human tier for all 15 factors (App. B, Table B.2; Sec. 5.1).

Top-label ECE depended on question form and task (SST-2 yes/no 0.091 underconfident, choice 0.020, AG News 0.089 with the middle of the scale overconfident: stated 0.750 vs observed 0.612 on 258 items); one fitted temperature cut held-out ECE to 0.023-0.034, and 71.6% of AG News answers sat at exactly 1.00; no directional calibration claim was possible for gpt-4.1-nano, while gpt-5.4-nano gave the true class zero probability on 216 of 284 errors (Tables 2-4, Sec. 4.1, 4.6).

The authors' WEV typed models had ECE 0.024-0.059 on browser steps and 0.033-0.099 out of domain, and a DONE-probability threshold trades premature stops against recall (WEV-4b 8.5% premature at 82% recall at 0.5; 3.8% at 67% at 0.8), but the BLOCKED (give-up) option was recalled on only 3% of 29 test steps for all three sizes (Tables 7, 10; Fig. 3; Sec. 5.4, 5.7). [Adjudicated: ECE <=0.06 in-domain, <=0.10 out of domain, no recalibration; DONE threshold works]

Jev's primary-class ECE was 0.049 against Laya's 0.322 (median confidence 0.41), while Qwen's three prompt-defined confidence levels gave 90.1% precision on 97.8% of rows; but Jev's fulfillment-mode ECE was 0.125 (report Sec. 9.1-9.3).

The paper reports ECE 0.0228 and Brier 0.0274 for the four-action Jev trading agent on 1,000 frozen BTCUSDT ticks (ECE 0.0546 / 0.0238 / 0.0240 by information level), but it does not define the outcome against which calibration was scored, the text and Table 2 disagree (0.0542/0.0306 vs 0.0546/0.0238), and the LLM comparison is modelled, not measured (Tables 2-3, 7; Sec. 4.1-4.2).

On 4,000 held-out domain names every probability band was right at least as often as stated, so the probability was conservative rather than calibrated (e.g. band 0.60-0.70: 95% interval of share right 74.5-82.6%; >= 0.95: 99.5% right at mean 0.98) (slide 9). [Adjudicated: Every band underconfident (0.60-0.70 band right 74.5-82.6%); conservative, not calibrated]

With one temperature per question type fitted on validation, held-out ECE is 0.006-0.035 on most tasks but 0.114 on the 12-way topic choice; the answer checker reaches ECE 0.013 only after training on 22,000 real judged Gemma 3 12B answers, having scored judge-correct and judge-wrong answers 0.89 vs 0.91 when trained on rule-made negatives (Sec. 4.3, 5.1-5.2, Fig. 4).

Called once per relation with only three English labels and no evidence, Jev chose the 'maybe' option for 1.0% (163/15,925) and 0.8% (196/24,800) of flagged Wikidata relations, and identical or symmetric inputs received different verdicts in 7/46 and 4/127 duplicate-triple groups and 18/1,836 and 22/445 reciprocal diplomatic-relation pairs; verdicts were never checked against human judgement (Sec. 4.1, 5.1, 5.5; Tables 3, 8).

On exact-target cases, Choice behaves as a step (a 45%->55% stated base rate raises it by 0.83-0.98 against a correct 0.10; holdout Brier 0.0665, temperature-scaled still 55x worse than Noul on base rates) while Noul stays within 0.015-0.027 of stated rates (normalized Noul Brier 0.0034 [0.003, 0.004]); on 650 human-vote items normalized Noul beats Choice (ChaosNLI Brier 0.096 vs 0.203) but neither beats a uniform guess on the most contested bin (0.135/0.321 vs 0.058), and the open Laya, Qwen3-0.6B PSR-FT and eve-rlcd models ignore stated rates (jump <=0.06) (Sec. 4.2-4.4, 5; Tables 3-6).

After per-type temperature scaling, sealed-set confidence 84.7% matches accuracy 82.6% (ECE 0.043, n=386) and ECE is 0.060/0.070 on unseen Banking77/CLINC150 label sets, but on 56 held-out multi-step items confidence is 70.8% against 48.2% accuracy (ECE 0.282); the abstain head separates the 15 unsupported items only when supervised (AUROC 0.82 [0.70, 0.93] vs 0.46 [0.32, 0.60]) and ranks CLINC150 out-of-scope queries (AUROC 0.97) while staying below 0.5, so it needs a tuned threshold (Sec. 5.2, 6.2; Tables 1, 3).

Over 14,642 moves in its own gridworld games, jev-1.13.0 gave chosen moves a mean probability of 0.72 while 51% were optimal (ECE 0.21; Brier 0.283 vs 0.250 for a constant), though moves at >=0.9 were optimal 74% of the time vs 42% below and its exam ECE was 0.06; the chat model Qwen3.5-4B read through option-number probabilities had ECE 0.06 and was the only model beating a constant (Brier 0.232 vs 0.249), while open Laya (ECE 0.13) and GLiClass (0.33) were also worse than a constant (Sec. 5.7; Fig. 6; App. B, H7). [Adjudicated: ECE 0.21, Brier 0.283 worse than constant; only generative Qwen beats constant]

With temperatures per question type fitted on validation, register-labelled test ECE was 0.002/0.007 (H2 met) and dangerous yes/no errors were 12 of 2,178 (0.6%) on the Austrian reference set, but 10 of the 12 were given with confidence >=0.9, the explicit abstention left 99.9% of Austrian questions answered, and minimum signers derived from the model's own coalition answers reached only 77.7% (H16 not met) (Sec. 5, 7; Table 3; App. A).

Decomposing each definition into criterion questions combined by a fixed rule improved macro-F1 in 6 of 30 comparisons and lowered it in 11 (HateCheck: 3 losses of 10, no gains), e.g. Laya -12.1 on Dynamic, Decider -34.0 on HateCheck, Jev +1.6 on Dynamic (matched by a tuned threshold, both .845), at 64-139% more Jev cost; component answers show which criterion decided a verdict but not which answer was wrong, and no gain was supported for either commercial LLM (Sec. 4.3-4.4, Table 4; App. G).

Moving feasibility checks out of the engine into a public gate raised Jev's placement correctness from 29/120 to 84/120 (+45.8 pp [37.5, 54.2]), the highest of five engines (52-71/120). Gains were smaller with shared quotas (14 to 42/120, below GLM-4.7-Flash's 50) and with fault-domain separation (6 to 45/120, below Gemini's 61), against 120/120 for a full deterministic rule. The intervention also changes instructions and refresh; only 9/139 surveyed families distinguish format, task and outcome gates (Tables III, XII, XX).

Exposing only the active behaviour-tree node's fields raised correct joint typed decisions from 90/120 (global interface) to 113/120, against 68/120 for prompt-matched constrained autoregressive decoding, and closed-loop success from 0/30 to 18/30, keeping decision errors separable from execution failures; the gain depends on a hand-built tree with predefined, mutually compatible candidates, and the 120 states repeat across seeds so counts are descriptive (Sec. IV-B, IV-D, VI).

Formal paper: if per-decision confidences from a model such as Jev's Noul in JEVDB are calibrated, lineage-weighted expected error predicts a query's output quality without labels, and a worked example shows an operator-level recall of 0.88 becoming an output-level recall of 0.58; calibration is assumed, no typed model is measured, and simulations are synthetic (Sec. 1, 4, 9).

Composing atomic Jev judgments by fixed rules lowered average macro-F1 from 62.93% to 57.31% (decomposition only, lower on 7 of 8 datasets) and to 62.00% when fused with the direct answer; appending judgments to the state along three paths gave 61.61%, gaining on four datasets but losing 10.47 points on E-c, so the decomposed chains were inspectable but not more accurate, about level with LLM chain-of-thought (62.91% average over five LLMs) (Sec. 4.3-4.4; Tables 2-3).

Keeping per-question Yes probabilities exposed which identity and relation conditions a candidate failed in one post-hoc case where the holistic 27B score chose the human's last-ranked image (Fig. 3), but the arithmetic mean lets strong scores compensate for a failed critical condition and identity risk was not reduced (47.62%); no systematic test of the audit trail (Sec. 3.5, 5.3, 7).

In two Human-Gated live calls (requested jev-latest, resolved jev-1.13.0) the four-label decisions (SUFFICIENT 0.86 with confidence 0.82; INSUFFICIENT 1.00) were persisted with raw-response hashes and both decision paths were RECONSTRUCTED, but only inside a consumer-built deterministic shell (prechecks, contract validation, evidence persistence; 124/124 offline tests, 0 fail-open across 20 injected failure cases), and the output carried no reasons; n=2, one call each (README 'J6 Bounded Live Observations'; J6 Closeout Sec. 5-7; J4_Implementation).

A Jev pre-screen in front of an LLM safety reviewer kept the in-sample miss rate (11.6%) at tau=0.1 while passing 65.6% of traffic on, but cut cost by only 4.3% once its own tokens were counted (tau=0.05 cost 4.7% more); thresholds chosen on held-out halves added at least one extra miss in 47% of splits (5% FNR target, p95 up to 16.7%), and a Laya-to-Jev confidence cascade lowered accuracy from 76.7% to 70.7% (Sec. 6, Tables 2 and 8).

Selective automation (1 - normalised AUGRC) was 0.935 for Jev 1.13, level with GLM 5.3 (0.936), below Gemini 3.8 Flash (0.964) and GPT-5.6 Sol (0.943) and above DeepSeek V4 Pro (0.862); open typed models ranged 0.365-0.866; the axis also rewards accuracy and no escalation target was tested (Table 3, Sec. 5).

Escalating the 20% least confident questions to Gemma-4-31B raised macro accuracy over seen and held-out tasks from 59.5 to 68.4 (S-PubMedBERT C, CE) and from 64.3 to 69.1 (Laya-large), above Gemma alone (62.1), but the budget was fixed retrospectively on the test set and not validated as a deployment threshold (Sec. 6.4, Fig. 3).

When a label contradicted its definition the models' own confidence ranked their errors the wrong way (AUROC 0.2433 laya-td, 0.1940 laya-en vs 0.8123 and 0.8236 under aligned labels), so an accept-when-confident gate would forward correct items and accept wrong ones; a two-rendering disagreement check instead raised laya-td accuracy on retained items from 0.7420 to 0.8921 at 0.8100 coverage (Sec. 5.8, Table 6; Sec. 6, Table 8).

In an exploratory analysis of cached predictions, referring Laya's 20% lowest-margin texts to GPT-6 Sol raised macro-F1 from .658 to .729 (Dynamic), .696 to .721 (MHS) and .730 to .763 (HateXplain), but referring them to GPT-5.6 Luna lowered HateXplain to .714; the fraction was not chosen on development data and the cascade stayed below Sol alone on Dynamic (.897) and HateXplain (.776) (App. I; Table 4).

Rejection thresholds calibrated on 80 pairs in one task exceeded 5% target false rejection in 6 of 12 transfers for each of Jev and Laya: Jev's DBpedia threshold rejected 69.3% [62.0, 76.5] of covered Emotion inputs, and its Emotion threshold (tau=1.00) disabled rejection on every target, recoverable only with target labels (82.5%/3.3% after AG News recalibration) (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 2). [Adjudicated: Gate thresholds fail 6/12 transfers; restored only by target recalibration (Sec. 3.1)]

On 100 BrowseComp-Plus questions run once, dual-system agents that accept confident SearchJev decisions and delegate the rest to Qwen3.5-27B reached 46.0% (0.8B) and 54.0% (4B) accuracy, against 45.0% for the System-2-only agent and 46.0% with Jev 1.13 in the System-1 slot. Median active time was 868-1102 s vs 4080 s. However, the gate threshold cannot be recovered from the logs and no explicit System-2 short-decision calls were recorded, so the contribution of escalation is unverified (Tables 4 and 8, App. D.3). [Adjudicated: Agents beat System-2-only but zero escalation calls logged, delta unrecoverable (Table 8)]

At the preregistered 0.97 retention bar the confidence-gated cascade from CLM to Qwen3-32B escalated 0.923-1.000 of items, the items it kept cost 0.009-0.019 accuracy against the strong judge alone, random escalation at the matched fraction performed comparably, and at the 0.10 error target no acceptance rule produced a threshold on 5 of 6 benchmarks; the one RM-Bench threshold accepted at most six items when transferred (Sec. 5-6, Table 4).

In a fixed-score replay of 15 saved Stack states, letting the model's own typed completion field control progression ended the task prematurely in 10/15 states, and in 120 closed-loop manipulation episodes external simulator postconditions blocked 7 of 8 model completion requests; acting on the typed decision was safe only because an independently built check held authority (Sec. IV-C, IV-G).

On 250 held-out CLINC150 items, escalating the least-confident items from kev-0.8B to kev-4B beat every re-ask scheme at matched cost (0.684 at 1.28 units vs 0.668 at 1.44; 0.760 at 2.40 vs 0.652 at 2.00) and reached 9B single-shot accuracy at 1.0-6.3 forward units instead of 11 on seven sources; the kev gate beat random routing by 2.0-7.2 points on four sources but the decider gate did not on every source, so the gate must be validated per model and dataset (Sec. 5.2, Table 2, Table 4).

Accepting only Jev Choice decisions with confidence >= 0.8 covered 71.9% of ModerationBench items at 94.3% accuracy (86.7% overall) and 48.7% of held-out PluRule decisions at 84.5% (69.5% overall), but the accepted sets were only 75.8% accurate on HateModerate and 67.6% on the PluRule test set, and Laya's gate retained only 2.0-19.2% of decisions (Sec. 4.3, Table 8; App. B.1).

Proves that escalation bands calibrated on a plan's own candidates (JEVDB's quality-controlled mode) make selection pushdown not quality-sound, and in synthetic simulations per-tuple escalation pricing met an output target at 1.9-5.3x lower cost than the best operator-level band while a simulated overconfident model predicted about 0.98 precision for databases delivering 0.87; no real engine or Jev data (Prop. 5.11, Sec. 9, Figs. 6-7).

The prospectively specified gate (consult a GPT-4.1-mini trace when Jev's Choice probability is below 0.8) had nothing to correct: Jev matched 95/96 keys, all 12 consulted questions were already right, the one error had probability exactly 0.8 and passed the gate, and executed fallback changed matches by -1.56 pp [-4.17, 0] (Sec. IV, Table III).

Escalating Jev's 25% least-certain reranking pairs to Qwen3-32B never helped: the gated labels lost 0.047 NDCG@10 [0.013, 0.084] to Jev alone at 80,000 answers and differed by -0.007 [-0.027, 0.012] at 160,000; Qwen's labels on uncertain pairs recovered 0.004 of the 0.050 lost by dropping 20% of pairs (Sec. 6; App. N); offline label allocation, not a deployed gate.

Deferring the 30% least-confident decisions to reasoning Qwen3.6 beat random deferral by +0.13 [0.08, 0.18] with actor and rate chosen on held-out games (+0.08 [0.02, 0.14] with shuffled options) and matched the thinker alone at 30% of its calls (0.75 vs 0.69, +0.06 [-0.02, 0.11]), but gave nothing for Kev 9B and Strands (AUROC 0.61, 0.60) and never beat the better component (+0.05 [-0.12, 0.11]); in 33 closed-loop games a fixed explore rule behind the same gate covered as much ground (Tables 3-4, Sec. 5.3-5.4).

With zero-shot Laya grounding plan steps (accept at p >= 0.4 with a word match or p >= 0.8, else lexical fallback, else LLM replan), plan-and-execute matched budget-matched ReAct (88.8% vs 92.0%, paired -3.2 pp [-7.7, +1.2]) at 83.6% fewer input tokens over 2,400 runs, but Laya was not significantly better than word-overlap matching (+2.3 pp [-0.2, +5.0]), declined every candidate on unlabeled TodoMVC toggles, and its post-action check never fired in 403 steps (Tables 1-2, Sec. 6-7).

A 5% automatic tier certified for Jev in 0 of 2,000 AG News splits (DeBERTa -c 23, task-exposed 95) but in 191 of 2,000 SST-2 splits (9.4% traffic automated), conformal single-label answers were wrong 5.93% at a nominal 5%, and 0.01 quantisation left a threshold only 53 operating points, although Jev's risk-coverage area beat -c by 1.81 points [0.84, 2.79] (Tables 5, 9; Sec. 4.4-4.5).

Only Jev supported an auto-accept gate: at cutoff 0.94 it accepted 86.5% of rows at 96.7% observed precision (Wilson lower bound >= 95%), whereas no Qwen bucket and no Laya cutoff reached 95%; the cutoff was fitted on the same 741 gold rows, and a spec rule queuing any flag cut automation from 91.9% to 26.6% (README Sec. 1, 5; report Sec. 9.2, 9.6).

A gate fixed on 1,000 separate names (keep Jev's rerank at p >= 0.62, else dksplit's first reading) raised held-out accuracy from 90.0% to 92.8% (178 corrected vs 65 broken, McNemar p = 2.5e-13), beat dksplit at every threshold from 0.30 to 0.98, and at p >= 0.90 accepted 53.1% of names at 99.2% precision (slides 6-8).

Used as a filter on 2,000 real Gemma 3 12B answers, the checker at threshold 0.5 catches 81% of wrong answers while keeping 68% of correct ones, raising shown-answer quality from 0.44 to 0.68 (0.81 at 0.7 with 14% shown), but it works only after training on real judged errors and judges answers with one changed number correctly only 45% of the time; the proposed show/retrieve/'I don't know' bands (0.6/0.3) were not evaluated (Sec. 5.2, Fig. 5).

In simulated shadow-mode response the fine-tuned detector blocked every attacker (1.00) within a minute, but caused 17 +/- 25 wrongful isolations and 5.5 estimated wrongful block hours per replication; because its false alarms carried high risk scores, risk-scaled cooldowns lengthened wrongful blocking (5.5 vs 2.9 h fixed), so the author keeps shadow mode with human approval as default (Tables 5-6, Sec. 5.5).

Answering only the most confident half of the sealed set gives 96.9% accuracy (89.6% at 80% coverage), but on held-out multi-step items the model is right about a third of the time between 0.5 and 0.9 stated confidence, so a threshold below 0.9 does not route them away, and head disagreement detects errors worse than maximum probability (AUROC 0.59 vs 0.81 for the released model) (Sec. 5.2; Fig. 5; Table A4).

As a typed per-turn supervisor mapping eight Noul/Choice/Score judgments to fixed controls for a claude-sonnet-5 coding agent on held-out SWE-bench Verified tasks, active Jev resolved 62.3% vs 55.1% unsupervised (+7.2 pp, 95% CI -4.3 to +18.8, n=69, p=.332), while a no-message shadow arm was +8.5 pp over none (CI 0.0 to +16.9, n=71, post hoc) and active only +1.6 pp over shadow (CI -6.5 to +9.7, n=62), so no intervention effect was resolved (Sec. 5.1-5.2; Table 2).

Learn-then-Test abstention thresholds fitted on Norwegian and Austrian validation held observed risk to 1.3% at 99.9% coverage against a 2% target on Austria (H22 met), but on the unseen Danish register they certified answering everything and the observed risk was 14.3% against a 5% target (H18 not met), with errors at high confidence (Sec. 7; Fig. 1; App. A, Table 7).

On HateCheck Jev cost $0.033 per 1,000 texts at 336 ms median vs $0.120/844 ms (Luna) and $1.177/1,426 ms (Sol), scoring 1.6 macro-F1 points below Sol at about 97% lower cost; the authors make use conditional on validation against a sample annotated under the platform's own policy and note HateCheck is constructed, not everyday traffic (Sec. 4.4, 5; App. H Table 9). [Adjudicated: $0.033/1K, 336 ms vs $0.120-1.177, 844-1426 ms; 1.6 F1 below Sol, no training]

Jev predicted 277,500 SocioBench respondent-question pairs at 37.69% accuracy, against 37.90% for non-thinking DeepSeek-V4-Flash, at 0.50 s vs 174.0 s per item (Table 5). It agreed less with a reference interest profiler (Jaccard 53.88% vs 65.24-65.86%; Table 4). The authors' InnerJev-27B voter agents called 47/51 states vs 46/51 for GPT-4o-mini agents, but with about twice the vote-share error (MAE 6.52 vs 3.06 pp) and a Democratic bias of +3.73 vs +2.31; two preliminary hosted-Jev runs also overestimated Harris (Sec. 5.4.3, Table 40).

In deployment, hosted Jev's labels alone leaked all four tested private attributes (100% coverage and accepted accuracy on 200 states each), and repeated interval queries recovered 10 privacy-related facts that GPT-6 declined to give directly. Jev also served as an oracle that raised the judged harmfulness of 100 harmful plans from 2.3 to 4.5 (100% success), and 200 of its labels trained a NanoJev surrogate from 49% to 92% agreement; NanoJev membership inference reached a mean ROC-AUC of 0.64 (Tables III, V, Sec. IV-A4, App. C).

Across seven political-science replications scored against human benchmarks, Jev matched or approached GPT-6 Luna and Qwen3.8-27B. It was worse on 2023 tweet relevance (76.2% vs 84.2%) and sentiment (rho 0.740 vs 0.816/0.841) and better on V-Dem (0.68 vs 0.63/0.59) and attack type. It took 0.09-0.27 s per decision vs 0.75-1.04 s for Luna, but was not cheaper than Luna at batch prices (Luna cheaper on 6 of 7 tasks). Its architecture, base model and training data are undisclosed (Tables 1-2, 9-10, App. E).

Jev's projected full-workload cost was $104.89 on ESCI (2.62M items) and $223.16 on RAID (5.62M) against $17,273 for zero-shot Opus 5 on ESCI, but with lower quality (0.531 vs 0.609), and agent-built artifacts reached 94% of Jev's ESCI score at 25% of its cost ($26.28) and 97% of its RAID AUROC at about 2% ($4.69); Jev cannot do generative extraction (MAVE) (Sec. 1, 4.2, Fig. 3, App. E).

Jev labels cost $1.97 and about 16 min of API time for 126,270 chess responses (7.6 ms/response, 20 concurrent) vs 1.91 H200 GPU-h for Qwen3-32B, and a reranker trained on Jev labels matched Qwen's (NDCG@10 0.637 vs 0.630, +0.008 [-0.007, 0.022]) from 21 min vs 5.1 GPU-h; but in chess a Jev-only evaluator added +2.8 Elo [-5.5, 11.0] over the stronger baseline vs +16.7 [9.0, 24.4] for Qwen, and Jev-trained scores weakened Othello and Connect-4 (Sec. 5.1, 6, 8, Table 4, App. G). [Adjudicated: Cheap labels; reranker matches but chess +2.8 vs +16.7, Othello/Connect-4 weakened]

Mean latency was 118 ms for Chip and 1,510 ms for JEV vs 4,631-16,009 ms for flagship LLMs, but JEV failed 678 of 5,000 records and reached 84.52% FFD exact match vs 98.32-99.12% for the flagships, and Chip's 99.32% needed task training on 88,604 records (Tables 3, 6, 9; Sec. 3.2.1). [Adjudicated: Faster, but JEV 678/5000 failures, 84.52% FFD; Chip needs task training]

190,582 Jev requests cost US$18.69 (0.19 s mean, 0.26 s p95; about US$3.40 per unit-year at 15-min checks) vs about 2 s per window for local Qwen2.5 72B at no per-query cost but with data kept on site, and the study confines the model to ranking candidate faults from code-computed features with recalibration and an operator's final call (Sec. 4.7, 5.4). [Adjudicated: 0.19 s, $18.69 vs local 72B 2 s, data on site; needs recalibration and operator]

Jev read 229,510 sampled narratives of a 5,018,080-crash population (reading all would cost about $773), and a second blinded human tier agreed with all 15 statewide counts within its margin (phone use 15,074 vs check 16,211 [13,050, 19,371]), but only after per-factor human recalibration that carries most of the variance (95% for alcohol, 99% for wrong-way) (Tables 2, 4; Sec. 5.1-5.2).

Jev classified 41,172 OpenAlex works to build a 14,714-work AI-research panel for 25 Indian institutions at about 13.5% annual growth, but its only check is an 88-record agent-adjudicated set (90.9% agreement overall, 97.2% on the 72 records at p >= 0.75), and admitting lower-confidence labels changes the total by +49.8% (Tables 1, 3; Sec. 2.4, 3.5).

As a stand-in for crowd vote distributions, Choice reports 0.80 where the ChaosNLI majority holds 45% and 0.88 on DICES-350 safety items split 55/45 and is worse than a uniform guess on every DICES measure (Brier 0.092 vs 0.071); normalized Noul is closer (ChaosNLI Brier 0.096 vs uniform 0.240) but loses to uniform on DICES KL (0.226 vs 0.158) and on contested items, and one fitted temperature equalizes the two only on average while under-confident on clear items (Sec. 4.4; Table 5; App. E, Table 8).
